abstract: Animal populations globally are suffering significant declines; many species are social, and individuals are likely to adjust their social behaviour as they lose associates. Therefore, social networks may respond to population decline as individuals adjust their social connections in response to changing social environments. Our understanding of how individual responses to loss of their associates alters the structure of their social networks is rudimentary. To quantify how social responses to individual loss can alter network structure, we simulated individual loss and compensatory formation of new social ties across 268 empirical animal social networks. Compensation changed the structural effects of individual loss, though these effects often depended on which individuals were removed. Loss of central, peripheral or random individuals produced different network responses, while social compensation had similar effects regardless of compensation strategy. Together, these results suggest that compensatory social behaviour can reorganise social networks as populations decline, even if departing from the original structure. Accounting for these responses may improve predictions of how demographic change affects social structure, particularly when losses are socially patterned and without knowing the compensation strategy. Broadly, our findings highlight compensation as a potentially important process linking individual social behaviour to the reorganisation of animal societies.
